extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, logic, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing and constructing inductive inferences, the role of syllogistic premises, axioms, and hypotheses in scientific reasoning; focused on when general and particular assertions are justified by experience. Useful for analyzing philosophical accounts of the scientific method and inductive justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience as the common ground of general and particular assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Both a universal generalization (e.g., 'All men are mortal') and the particular application (e.g., 'Socrates is mortal') are justified by the same grounds of experience; the evidence that supports the general statement also supports its application to individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues that the major and the particular are proved together by the experiential grounds on which the general assertion was formed. This rebuts the view that the major alone proves the minor; instead both draw their warrant from the same experiential basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the minor premise: showing the required likeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The minor premise identifies that the new individual is 'like' the observed cases (has the marks required by the general formula) and thus falls under the predicate of the major.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The syllogistic minor is not logically necessary but is the practical step that indicates the comparison has been made. It specifies the precise kind of likeness required to bring an unobserved case within the same predicate and is a precaution against erroneous inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogistic premises are methodological conveniences, not logical necessities
rubrics_metrics.description: Major and minor premises (in their formal syllogistic shape) are not essential conditions of reasoning; they are conventions that help record and check inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning from particulars to particulars can be performed without expressing syllogistic premises; converting a rough inference into a careful one often consists merely in selecting two syllogistic premises for clarity and record-keeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses and conditionality of conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific 'hypotheses' are often assumptions not literally true in all respects; reasoning from such assumptions yields conclusions that are conditional rather than categorical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill distinguishes hypotheses used as idealizations (e.g., in geometry) from conjectures meant to be literally true. One must bear in mind the hypothetical element—that what is taken as exactly true may be an approximation—and treat consequent conclusions as conditional on the assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms as inductive generalizations from experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometrical and mechanical axioms originate in experience; they are generalizations suggested and repeatedly confirmed by observation rather than purely a priori truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill and cited authorities argue that axioms carry their inductive origin on their face: simple, universal propositions about magnitude and mechanics are suggested continually by experience and are accepted because of their persistent confirmation in observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by approximation (method of concomitant variations / limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: When idealized concepts (e.g., perfectly straight lines) do not appear in experience, we justify axioms about them by observing a series of approximations and inferring the limit-case result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: as empirical lines become nearer to the ideal of 'no breadth or flexure', the space-inclosing power of two such lines approaches zero; from this concomitant variation one inductively infers the ideal-limit proposition (doctrine of limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity, universality, and obviousness as evidentiary marks of axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Necessary, universal truths are typically simple, intelligible, and continually suggested by experience; these qualities make their verification obvious and ensure widespread assent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill contends that if a truth is simple, universally suggested by experience, and verifiable in every instance, it becomes part of the mental picture of the object and commands implicit assent, eliminating occasion for exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish practical inference from scientific induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Many everyday inferences from particular cases to particular cases (practical inference) are intellectually similar to induction but are made without explicit formulation of general laws; scientific induction requires passing through a general proposition for record and justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues against restricting 'induction' to formally recorded generalizations: informal practical inferences can exhibit comparable intellectual quality, though science needs general formulations for transmissible knowledge and verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary risk of fallibility occurs at the initial axiomatic assumption; longer chains add oversight risk
rubrics_metrics.description: If a fundamental axiom is fallible, the risk is incurred at the first use of that axiom; repeating the same axiom in subsequent steps does not multiply that intrinsic risk, though longer argument chains increase chances of casual errors (carelessness, ambiguous terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responding to objections that longer heterogeneous arguments compound risk, Mill notes that while oversights and ambiguous terminology can cause errors in long trains of reasoning, these are distinct dangers from the grounding-postulate's intrinsic fallibility and typically arise from human error rather than logical multiplication of risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate theoretical compatibility: description vs literal claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Different explanations of the same phenomena may be compatible if one is a descriptive or representational device while another asserts a literal material mechanism; incompatibility arises when competing theories make directly contradictory material claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill uses the example of the vortex theory and Newtonian centripetal force: as long as the earlier theory can be reformulated to produce the same effects (i.e., as a representation), it may be reconcilable with the later theory; but if it asserts mutually exclusive material entities, conflict remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mental imagery and recollection as legitimate sources of evidence where reliable
rubrics_metrics.description: In some domains (notably simple geometrical forms) recollection and mental images are sufficiently precise to serve as bases for experiment-like inferences when the objects themselves are absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill notes that mental images of lines, circles, and rectangles are generally distinct and can be examined; for other senses (color, odor) recollection is less reliable and varies among individuals, so the evidentiary weight differs by subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check applicability of idealized axioms to real physical cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Axioms often rely on idealizations (e.g., lines without breadth, perfectly rigid levers); when applying such axioms to real-world cases, one must consider the physical properties and approximations that justify treating the ideal as representative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill discusses statics axioms and points out that mechanical proofs implicitly rely on assumptions about thickness, material composition, and molecular behavior; experimental corroboration in ordinary life often supplies the background justification even without direct formal trials.
